findings.explanation: Deetjen's 'private economic loss' is a private net present value that counts the heat pump's net capital cost as well as energy cost (the paper's method, NPVprivate with Kheatpump). The sentence says only 'economic loss' and 'often economical', so in an article whose question is running cost a reader takes it as a heat pump costing more to run than oil. The assertion's qualification claims 's19 and s20 both name their measure as counting equipment cost'; s20 does not.
findings.suggestion: Name the measure in the sentence, e.g. 'counting the cost of buying the heat pump over its life as well as the fuel, switching usually leaves an oil-heated homeowner worse off', so it reads as the lifetime-cost counterpart of s19 and not as a running-cost result.

findings.explanation: 'Anyone switching from baseboards will see significant savings on their power bill' is the report's own inference from an energy figure ('up to 65 per cent less energy', quoted from Natural Resources Canada); it measured no bills. Repeated without that note, the article endorses a universal bill claim the package contradicts: Wilson finds only 73-86% of homes heating with electricity, oil or propane without AC would have positive bill savings, most of the rest in hotter climates. The closing clause ('compares heat pumps with baseboards only') limits the fuel, not the 'anyone'.
findings.suggestion: Report the energy figure and say the bill saving is the report's inference from it, not a measurement, e.g. 'and infers from that significant savings on the power bill for those switching from baseboards'; drop 'anyone' or mark it as the report's word.

findings.explanation: The sentence says EnergySage 'states it without conditions', then quotes it saying 'almost everywhere', which is a condition. The framing contradicts the quotation it introduces.
findings.suggestion: Say 'states it most broadly' or 'with only an "almost"'.

findings.explanation: Table t2 (held unapproved): the 33% row does not state its baseline. In the CEE passage the ducted flex-fuel systems are measured against their propane furnace (baseline operation 97-98% propane), while the 53% row is against an assumed electric resistance heater; one 'Saving' column mixes two baselines, and a reader of a page about oil could take the 33% as against oil or as unexplained. The '$377-$764' ducted row likewise pools flex-fuel (propane baseline) and all-electric (resistance baseline) systems. The 33% also appears in no prose sentence. This finding sits on s07 as the first sentence of the section holding t2; s07 itself is approved.
findings.suggestion: Label the rows with their baselines ('Ducted flex-fuel systems vs the propane furnace, average cost saving'; 'All-electric systems vs assumed electric resistance'), and say in the caption or a row label that the dollar ranges mix the two baselines (or drop them).

findings.explanation: s19 brings a lifetime (net present) cost result into a running-cost article, but it names the measure up front ('counting what the equipment costs as well as the fuel'), and s24 keeps it apart ('the studies that count equipment cost'), so it does not stand in for a running-cost finding. RMI's result is modelled for Providence; the passage itself generalises to New England areas without gas, which the sentence follows. Approved.

Revision 2 answers the revision-1 t2 finding: each row now names its baseline (propane furnace for the 33% flex-fuel row, assumed electric resistance for the 53% and ductless rows), the pooled ducted dollar row says the baselines are mixed, and the caption says each row has its own baseline. t2 approved; the earlier warning on s07 is closed by this.
